<h2 class="sec">Center for Economic Mobility</h2>

I direct the Center for Economic Mobility at Rice University's Kinder Institute
for Urban Research, where we work with school districts, agencies, and community
organizations in the Houston area.

A research partnership pays for itself twice. It can help an institution decide
what to do next, and it can let economists ask questions they could not
otherwise ask. The two essays below take those returns in turn.

The test of learning is not whether we understand the past better. It is whether
the next decision is better because of it.

[Visit the Center for Economic Mobility →](https://kinder.rice.edu/center/center-economic-mobility){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

<h2 class="sec">Essays</h2>

::: {.entry}
[On Research and Development of Social Programs](research-and-development.html)

August 2026 · Written for the people who design, fund, and deliver programs

What a research partnership is for, and why doing and learning should not be
treated as competing objectives. Drawn from more than a decade with Alief
Independent School District, including the three years in which the project
served no families.

[PDF](papers/research-and-development.pdf)
:::

::: {.entry}
[On Research Partnerships and Economic Science](research-partnerships.html)

October 2026 · Written for economists

The second return. Partnerships can do more than estimate whether a program
works: by generating the right experimental variation, they can make structural
models easier to falsify. Drawn from the randomized evaluation of JumpStart.

[PDF](papers/research-partnerships.pdf)
:::
